guided.title: Profile a raw table
guided.prompt: The text `RAW` is read as strings. Print three lines: the shape as a tuple, the number of exact duplicate rows, and the number of missing values in the whole table (`raw.isna().sum().sum()`).

import io
import pandas as pd
RAW = "id,name,score\n1,Ann,5\n2,Bob,\n2,Bob,\n3,,7\n"
raw = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(RAW), dtype=str)

guided.title: Standardise names and codes
guided.prompt: Clean the `city` series: strip spaces, convert to upper case, and map the long name `"NEW YORK"` to `"NYC"` with `map` and a function using `dict.get`. Print the sorted distinct values as a list.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd
city = pd.Series([" new york", "NYC ", "Boston", "boston ", "New York"])
print(city.unique().tolist())
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd
city = pd.Series([" new york", "NYC ", "Boston", "boston ", "New York"])
names = {"NEW YORK": "NYC"}
clean = city.str.strip().str.upper().map(lambda v: names.get(v, v))
print(sorted(clean.unique().tolist()))
hints: Strip and upper-case first, so spellings can be compared.
`names.get(v, v)` returns the mapped value or the value itself.

guided.title: Money text to numbers
guided.prompt: Convert `price` (text such as `"$1,050.5"`, `"20"`, `"free"`) to numbers by removing `$` and commas and coercing failures. Print the list of numbers with `.tolist()` and then the number of failed conversions.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd
price = pd.Series(["$1,050.5", "20", "free", "$7"])
print(price.tolist())
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd
price = pd.Series(["$1,050.5", "20", "free", "$7"])
num = pd.to_numeric(price.str.replace("[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")
print(num.tolist())
print(num.isna().sum())
hints: Remove the characters that are not part of the number first.

guided.title: Keep the corrected row
guided.prompt: Table `t` has repeated `id` values where the later row is the correction. Keep one row per `id`, the last one, and print `print(t.to_string(index=False))` of the result (row order as in the input).
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd
t = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 1, 3], "price": [10, 20, 12, 30]})
print(t.to_string(index=False))
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd
t = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 1, 3], "price": [10, 20, 12, 30]})
t = t.drop_duplicates(subset="id", keep="last")
print(t.to_string(index=False))
hints: Use `subset` to name the key column and `keep` to choose which row survives.

independent.title: Clean an employee file
independent.prompt: The setup loads an employee file as text. Write the full cleaning: strip and title-case `name`; strip and upper-case `dept`; convert `salary` (remove `$` and commas) and `hired` (`%Y-%m-%d`) with `errors="coerce"`; drop exact duplicates, then keep the last row for each `emp_id`; reject rows with missing salary or hire date. Print four lines: rows read, rows kept, rows rejected, and the list of kept `emp_id` values.

import pandas as pd

E6,Gus Hall,Sales,0,2018-05-05
"""

independent.solution:
import io
import pandas as pd
RAW = """emp_id,name,dept,salary,hired
E1, ann lee ,sales,"$52,000",2021-03-01
E2,BOB KING,Sales ,48000,2020-07-15
E3,cara diaz,IT,"$61,500",2022-13-01
E2,BOB KING,Sales ,48000,2020-07-15
E4,Dan Fox,it,n/a,2019-11-30
E5,eve ray,HR,"$45,250.50",2023-01-20
E5,Eve Ray,hr,"$47,000",2023-01-20
E6,Gus Hall,Sales,0,2018-05-05
"""
raw = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(RAW), dtype=str)
df = raw.copy()
df["name"] = df["name"].str.strip().str.title()
df["dept"] = df["dept"].str.strip().str.upper()
df["salary"] = pd.to_numeric(df["salary"].str.replace("[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")
df["hired"] = pd.to_datetime(df["hired"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
df = df.drop_duplicates().drop_duplicates(subset="emp_id", keep="last")
bad = df["salary"].isna() | df["hired"].isna()
clean, rejects = df[~bad], df[bad]
print(len(raw))
print(len(clean))
print(len(rejects))
print(clean["emp_id"].tolist())

import io
import pandas as pd
RAW = """emp_id,name,dept,salary,hired
E1, ann lee ,sales,"$52,000",2021-03-01
E2,BOB KING,Sales ,48000,2020-07-15
E3,cara diaz,IT,"$61,500",2022-13-01
E2,BOB KING,Sales ,48000,2020-07-15
E4,Dan Fox,it,n/a,2019-11-30
E5,eve ray,HR,"$45,250.50",2023-01-20
E5,Eve Ray,hr,"$47,000",2023-01-20
E6,Gus Hall,Sales,0,2018-05-05
"""
raw = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(RAW), dtype=str)
df = raw.copy()
df["name"] = df["name"].str.strip().str.title()
df["dept"] = df["dept"].str.strip().str.upper()
df["salary"] = pd.to_numeric(df["salary"].str.replace("[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")
df["hired"] = pd.to_datetime(df["hired"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
df = df.drop_duplicates().drop_duplicates(subset="emp_id", keep="last")
bad = df["salary"].isna() | (df["salary"] <= 0) | df["hired"].isna()
clean = df[~bad]
assert clean["emp_id"].is_unique
assert (clean["salary"] > 0).all()
avg = clean.groupby("dept")["salary"].mean().round(2)
print(avg.to_string())
print("ok")

independent.solution:
import numpy as np
import io
import pandas as pd
RAW = """emp_id,name,dept,salary,hired
E1, ann lee ,sales,"$52,000",2021-03-01
E2,BOB KING,Sales ,48000,2020-07-15
E3,cara diaz,IT,"$61,500",2022-13-01
E2,BOB KING,Sales ,48000,2020-07-15
E4,Dan Fox,it,n/a,2019-11-30
E5,eve ray,HR,"$45,250.50",2023-01-20
E5,Eve Ray,hr,"$47,000",2023-01-20
E6,Gus Hall,Sales,0,2018-05-05
"""
raw = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(RAW), dtype=str)
df = raw.copy()
df["salary"] = pd.to_numeric(df["salary"].str.replace("[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")
df["hired"] = pd.to_datetime(df["hired"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
df = df.drop_duplicates().drop_duplicates(subset="emp_id", keep="last")
bad_salary = df["salary"].isna() | (df["salary"] <= 0)
bad = bad_salary | df["hired"].isna()
rejects = df[bad].assign(reason=np.where(bad_salary[bad], "bad salary", "bad date"))
print(rejects[["emp_id", "reason"]].to_string(index=False))
independent.expected:
emp_id     reason
    E3   bad date
    E4 bad salary
    E6 bad salary

checks.question: Why standardise text (strip, case) before calling `drop_duplicates`?
options: Copies that differ only in spaces or capitals are not seen as duplicates
drop_duplicates only works on lower case
checks.explanation: `"UK "` and `"uk"` are different strings, so rows that are really copies survive until the text is standardised. `drop_duplicates` itself is case-sensitive but works on any text.

checks.question: `pd.to_numeric(pd.Series(['5', 'abc']), errors='coerce').isna().sum()` prints what?
checks.explanation: `abc` cannot be converted and becomes NaN, which `isna` counts once; `5` converts. Without `errors="coerce"` the call would raise an error.

checks.question: You read 100 rows, remove 5 duplicates and reject 8 rows. How many rows are kept?
checks.explanation: 100 minus 5 minus 8 is 87. Reconciling read = kept + rejected + duplicates is a simple check that no rows were lost silently.

checks.question: Order id 7 appears twice with different amounts and the later row is the correction. Which call keeps the correction?
checks.explanation: The default compares whole rows, so both rows differing in amount survive. `subset` names the key and `keep="last"` keeps the later row; `keep=False` would drop every row of the repeated key.

checks.question: What is the purpose of `assert clean['order_id'].is_unique` at the end of a pipeline?
options: It stops the run with an error if the key is not unique
checks.explanation: An assertion states a rule and fails loudly when it is broken. It does not change the data; the repair must happen in earlier steps.
